originalTitle: Jim Cramer Warns the Market Is “Destroying Savings for the Many”
summary: Americans over 70 own a bigger slice of the stock market than any other age group, and a few giant names now drive both the gains and the losses. Here is how retirees can check their own exposure before the next drop.
content:
On his Nov. 19, 2026, Mad Money broadcast, Jim Cramer described a problem many retirees can see in their account statements: “The market’s destroying savings for the many faster than it’s creating it for the few.” In the same segment, he acknowledged the market had slid into a bear market and called the dynamic “a very unhealthy relationship.”

The trading days since then have only added to his concern. The S&P 500 fell 8.56% in the week ended Nov. 20 and 10.77% over the past month. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 10.51% for the week and 16.1% for the month, which leaves it down 0.95% for 2026. On Nov. 20 alone, the S&P 500 lost 3.55%, and the Nasdaq 100 lost 5.67%. News coverage tied the plunge to a deepening tech selloff as the AI trade came apart, pushing the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year.

What Cramer Means by Savings for the Many

Major indexes are weighted by market value, so a handful of giant companies can carry the headline number while most stocks lag. That pattern has run for years. Over the past decade, the Nasdaq 100 gained 411.73%, while the small-cap Russell 2000 gained 93.23%.

The same concentrated winners are now leading the decline, and many savers who believe they are diversified through index funds own large amounts of them. Savings were already uneven before this selloff began. In 2024, the average Vanguard plan balance was $148,153, while the median was $38,176. A drawdown takes a much bigger bite out of that typical household’s cushion.

According to the Federal Reserve’s Distributional Financial Accounts , households aged 70 and older held 40.5% [ 1 ] of all household corporate equities and mutual fund shares in 2026 Q2. Households aged 55 to 69 held another 39.3% [ 1 ] . Households under 40 held just 5.7% [ 1 ] . The oldest group’s share has risen from 29.2% [ 1 ] in early 2020.

Many older savers also hold more stock than their age would suggest. Fidelity found that many 401(k) participants aged 55 and up carry equity allocations above its suggested glide path, and that 6.9% of savers in their 50s have all of their 401(k) savings in stocks. Retirees who are drawing down their accounts face sequence risk : when they sell shares at low prices to cover expenses, those losses become permanent.

Fear in the market is rising. The VIX reached 28.44 [ 2 ] on Nov. 19, up from 19.3 [ 2 ] on Nov. 13. University of Michigan consumer sentiment stood at 48.0 [ 3 ] in October, a historically low reading.

A Retirement Framework Worth Reviewing This Week

These steps are a framework for thinking through your own situation:

A VIX reading above 30 would signal high fear. Watch the next consumer sentiment release and whether the Nasdaq’s slide reaches official bear market territory. Retirees should also track how much of their withdrawal needs are covered by cash and income, rather than stock sales.

Cramer’s warning points to a market where gains piled up in a few names while risk spread to everyone else. The retirees best positioned to come through this selloff are the ones who never have to sell a falling stock to pay a bill, which is the whole point of the dividend ladder we laid out in a free guide here .

Chris Lange is a financial and geopolitical writer with more than a decade of experience covering a myriad of topics. He has published thousands of articles for 24/7 Wall St., with past coverage focused heavily on stocks, IPOs, healthcare, defense, global affairs, and technology.

His work has been quoted, or referenced by a number of outlets including Business Insider, USA Today, Yahoo Finance, MSN, The Motley Fool, and many other publications. A graduate of Southwestern University, he studied business with a focus on investments and has previous experience in banking and startups.

When not reading or writing the news, he is following his passion for Lacrosse, playing chess, or building solar projects with his dad.
